strengths: Comprehensive theoretical contribution: The paper provides the first simultaneous best-of-both-worlds guarantees achieving first-order, second-order, and path-length regret bounds in the adversarial regime, along with variance-adaptive gap-independent and gap-dependent bounds in the stochastic regime.

Dual algorithmic paradigms: Both global optimization (over the occupancy measure polytope) and local policy optimization (per-state OFTRL with dilated exploration bonuses and a novel optimistic Q-estimator) are thoroughly analyzed, giving practitioners and theorists insights into trade-offs between computational tractability and minimax rates.

Technical innovation in estimator design: The introduction of a controlled optimistic Q-function estimator in policy optimization successfully corrects the bias from loss predictors while preserving variance reduction, solving a key challenge in best-of-both-worlds policy optimization.

Complementary lower bounds: The authors establish lower bounds for data-dependent measures (first-order, second-order, path-length, and variance-dependent), confirming that the global optimization bounds are minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors (with the known gap for path length matching bandits).

Clear presentation and extensive appendix: The paper is clearly structured, well-contextualized with existing literature via comparison tables, and includes complete, rigorous mathematical proofs in the appendix.
weaknesses: Known transition assumption: The results strictly assume known transition dynamics. While this is a standard and justifiable setting for establishing foundational data-dependent guarantees, extending these techniques to unknown transitions remains an unresolved challenge.

Trade-off between path-length and variance-dependent bounds: As noted in the paper, attaining either path-length bounds or variance-aware gap-dependent bounds requires selecting different loss prediction schemes ($m_t$ via gradient descent vs. empirical mean), meaning a single parameterization does not simultaneously adapt to both.

Sub-optimal horizon dependence in policy optimization: The policy optimization bounds suffer an extra multiplicative factor of $H$ in comparison to global optimization, a known open challenge in adversarial MDP policy optimization.

strengths: First comprehensive framework providing second-order ($Q_\infty$) and path-length ($V_1$) data-dependent regret guarantees for online episodic tabular MDPs, extending classical bandit results to the structured RL setting.

For global optimization, the stochastic gap-dependent regret bound improves upon Jin et al. (2021) by adapting to variance and eliminating the undesirable dependence on $1 / \min_{s,a} \Delta(s,a)$.

Introduces novel technical mechanisms, notably an optimistic Q-function estimator in policy optimization designed to balance prediction-induced bias against variance reduction, and clean dilated bonus handling.

Complements upper bounds with information-theoretic lower bounds establishing the near-optimality of the global optimization bounds with respect to $L^\star$, $Q_\infty$, $V_1$, and the occupancy-weighted variance $\mathbb{V}$.
weaknesses: The analysis assumes known transition dynamics $P$; extending these refined data- and variance-dependent bounds to unknown transitions remains an unresolved and challenging open problem.

The algorithm requires choosing between two different loss prediction mechanisms ($m_t$ via gradient descent vs. empirical mean) depending on whether one desires path-length bounds or variance-adaptive gap-dependent bounds, rather than achieving all guarantees simultaneously under a single specification.

Policy optimization results incur an additional factor of $\sqrt{H}$ compared to the global optimization bounds (a well-known bottleneck in adversarial policy optimization, but still a sub-optimality).
The submission is purely theoretical with no synthetic or empirical simulations illustrating the practical behavior or running time of the proposed algorithms.

strengths: Comprehensive theoretical contribution: The paper provides the first second-order ($Q_\infty$) and path-length ($V_1$) regret bounds for online episodic tabular MDPs under adversarial losses, as well as refined variance-adaptive bounds (both gap-independent and gap-dependent) in the stochastic-with-corruptions regime.

Dual algorithmic frameworks: The authors develop both global optimization (occupancy-measure based) and policy optimization (dilated bonus and per-state updates) algorithms within the Optimistic FTRL (OFTRL) framework using log-barrier regularization.

Novel technical mechanisms: For policy optimization, the paper introduces a carefully crafted optimistic $Q$-function estimator that subtracts an exploration-scaled margin to strictly control bias while preserving variance reduction from loss predictions.

Near-matching lower bounds: The paper establishes information-theoretic lower bounds for tabular MDPs in terms of $L^*$, $Q_\infty$, $V_1$, and $\mathbb{V}$, proving that the global-optimization upper bounds are minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors (with the known $\sqrt{SA/H}$ path-length gap discussed).

Thorough and rigorous proofs: The supplementary material is extensive, clearly organized, and rigorously details all technical steps from OFTRL Bregman divergence analysis to self-bounding techniques and lower-bound constructions.
weaknesses: Known transition assumption: The entire framework assumes known transition dynamics $P$. While extending data-dependent and variance-adaptive bounds to unknown transitions is known to be very challenging, this restricts the immediate applicability to model-free settings.

Predictor trade-off / lack of complete unification: The path-length bound and the variance-aware gap-dependent bound require two different loss prediction mechanisms (gradient-descent predictor vs. empirical-mean predictor). Hence, a single algorithm instantiation does not simultaneously achieve all claimed data-dependent and variance-dependent bounds.

Suboptimal horizon scaling in policy optimization: As is standard in dilated-bonus policy optimization literature, the regret bounds incur an extra factor of $H$ (or $\sqrt{H}$) compared to the global optimization approach and lower bounds.

Minor typographic and labeling inconsistencies in the appendix: For example, Remark D.11 and Remark E.16 are headed as 'Restatement of Theorem 4.3', although in the main text they correspond to Remark 4.3 and Remark 5.4, and there are occasional minor indexing inconsistencies in Appendix G (e.g., notation around perturbed states $\tilde{s}$ and distributions).

strengths: First second-order and path-length bounds for online tabular MDPs: The paper extends data-dependent guarantees beyond standard first-order (small-loss) bounds to second-order fluctuation bounds ($Q_\infty$) and path-length bounds ($V_1$) in episodic tabular MDPs under bandit feedback.

Unified best-of-both-worlds (BOBW) framework: The proposed algorithms simultaneously achieve near-optimal data-dependent adversarial regret bounds and variance-aware gap-independent and gap-dependent bounds in the stochastic regime with adversarial corruptions, without requiring prior knowledge of the regime or problem parameters.

Comprehensive coverage of both algorithmic paradigms: The work successfully develops both global optimization (occupancy-measure based OFTRL with log-barrier regularizers and loss-shifting) and policy optimization (local OFTRL with dilated exploration bonuses, virtual episodes, and a novel optimistic Q-estimator) variants.

Novel technical contribution in policy optimization: To overcome bias introduced by loss predictions in OFTRL when lifting to Q-space, the paper designs an optimistic Q-function estimator with an explicit margin subtraction ($-\gamma_t H / q_t(s)$), guaranteeing controlled optimism in expectation while maintaining variance reduction.

Tightness backed by lower bounds: Information-theoretic lower bounds are established for the data-dependent adversarial quantities $\Omega(\sqrt{S A L^\star})$, $\Omega(\sqrt{S A Q_\infty})$, $\Omega(\sqrt{H V_1})$ and the stochastic variance measure $\Omega(\sqrt{S A V T})$, demonstrating near-optimality for the global optimization upper bounds.
Remarkably thorough and rigorous theoretical analysis: The 72-page manuscript provides complete, clear, and mathematically rigorous proofs for all lemmas, auxiliary statements, and main theorems.
weaknesses: Restriction to known transition dynamics: The entire analysis assumes known transition kernels $P$. While the authors clearly acknowledge this limitation and explain the technical hurdles of data-dependent transition estimation, extending these results to unknown transitions remains an important open challenge.

Discrepancy in the path-length bound: There remains a $\sqrt{S A / H}$ gap between the adversarial path-length upper bound $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{S A V_1})$ and the lower bound $\Omega(\sqrt{H V_1})$. While this gap is analogous to known issues in multi-armed bandits, narrowing it remains unresolved.

Extra factor of $H$ in policy optimization: As is common in policy optimization with dilated bonuses (e.g., Luo et al., 2021; Dann et al., 2023a), the regret bounds incur an additional factor of $H$ compared to global optimization, leaving closing the minimax $H$-gap open.

Lack of empirical evaluation: The paper is purely theoretical. While appropriate for a deep learning theory contribution, illustrative numerical simulations demonstrating the adaptivity of the predictors and learning rates on synthetic MDP benchmarks would have further enriched the presentation.
